edits.note: Tony, 13 Oct: "go with the first version" and "we expect to adopt this pattern (Happy main agent hold tools, then dispatch sub-agent to narrow tool selection to do their specific work)". The lookup is rewritten to it: the parent's own agent is allowed the reader's three Gmail read tools so that the reader it starts can use them, and is told never to call them itself. Also recorded: what the wave A runbook found about the gate, the token store and the wrapper, each waiting for his yes at its step A4.

set.how:
Connector: `gog mcp`, gog's own MCP server, as one host-side stdio entry under `mcp.servers` per parent, started with only that parent's token and narrowed with `--allow-tool` to the Gmail read tools; a read-only token each from `gog auth add` (`--services` Gmail only, `--gmail-scope readonly`). Reader: one generated `

-mail` agent per parent: `profile: "minimal"`, only `

-gmail__*` allowed (also in `tools.sandbox.tools`) and denied by name elsewhere, except on that parent's own agent once its lookup is on (see Lookup); memory search off; one cloud model, storage off, no fallback. Gate: the connector reaches Google and nothing else. The wave A runbook found that a firewall rule cannot name Google's hosts for this program, so it builds the gate as one firewall rule that blocks every direct connection by the connector plus a small local proxy that lets it reach three named Google hosts; Tony's yes to that is asked at the runbook's step A4. Text: one weekday 07:00 Eastern job per reader from the jobs script (G003), Gmail read tools only, delivered to its owner: own label, school lines first (F051), no links, medical mail by sender and subject only, silent on an empty morning. Lookup (Tony, 13 Oct): `

-main` hands a mail question to its own `

-mail` through `subagents.allowAgents`, with `subagents.requireAgentId: true` (the list governs only a call that names an agent; a call that names none would start a copy of the asking agent), with a two-minute default time limit. On 2026.9.7 an agent started by another keeps only the tools its asker is allowed (the asker's allowed tools and its denies are passed to the helper and applied last), so `

-main` is itself allowed the three `

-gmail` read tools (also in its sandbox tool list) and no longer denies that one server; its instructions tell it to hand every mail question to the reader and never to call those tools itself. The reader's own list, the three read tools and nothing else, is what narrows the hand-off. Eval-only copies of a parent's agent never hold a connector tool or the hand-off to a mail reader (except T5's throwaway pair in wave C, which reads only the test mailbox), so the lookup is tested live. House rules: adds the account-connector rule when that plugin is first created. From then the parent's own agent is blocked in code from calling the Gmail tools it holds, if test T5 shows that the check is told which agent is calling.
depends_on: G003 in its small form: the three scheduler switches and the short jobs script, which creates each 07:00 job with its owner's handle read from the family file. The job is made by that script, not by the scheduling tool, so Jordan's copy needs no command-owner right
gog installed at a pinned version, with its read-only, service and tool-filter options confirmed on the installed program
A Google Cloud project, sign-in client and consent screen published to In production: Tony sets these up by hand at execution
Each parent's own approval of read-only Gmail on Google's screen: Tony first, then Jordan, who has agreed

One firewall rule: the mail connector may reach Google and nothing else. Tony accepted on 12 Oct that mail is read with this one rule before the full firewall and the outbound proxy exist. The wave A runbook builds the gate as one blocking rule plus a small local proxy for the connector, because a firewall rule cannot name Google's hosts for this program; his yes to that is asked at its step A4
Tony provides at execution: a second Google account used only as a test mailbox for planted mail, and a capped model key for each mail reader
Tony provides at execution: the school senders' addresses, used as a hint in the job's message for the school lines (F051), not as a filter
The Zero Data Retention application to OpenAI filed and its date written down; mail does not wait for the answer (Tony, 12 Oct)
caveats: The read-only grant lets the connector read every message in the account. The school lines are picked out by the model, with no sender filter and no check, so it may miss a school mail or list one that is not; and mail that arrives during the day waits for the next morning's text.

Mail text goes to the cloud model on Tony's go-ahead of 12 Oct, and is read before the full firewall and the outbound proxy exist. Until OpenAI approves Zero Data Retention its abuse-monitoring log can keep that text for up to 30 days. Both points depart from the roadmap's rules for mail readers, by his choice.

Nothing about the connector has been tried on this Mac: gog is not installed, so its flags come from upstream docs, and whether a token from the published sign-in app outlives seven days on a personal account is test T1. If the day-8 search fails, the choice is a weekly sign-in per parent or a different connector.

'No links' and 'sender and subject only for medical mail' are instructions to the reader, not enforced limits. What limits harm is that the reader holds only Gmail read tools and its outputs are the scheduled text to its owner and, once the lookup is on, its answer to its owner's own agent.

The lookup goes two steps beyond the roadmap's mail design. Its answer comes back into the parent's own agent, which holds that parent's chats, can search the web and will later hand tasks to the web helper. And by Tony's decision of 13 Oct that agent is itself allowed the Gmail read tools, because a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed: an instruction, checked by a count of its tool calls, keeps it from reading mail itself, not a tool limit, until the house-rules plugin's check exists, and then only if test T5 allows that check. Only prompt rules and a seeded-mail test stand between them, so it goes live in its own step and can be switched off without touching the morning text.
Google's Gemini app already answers questions from a person's own Gmail and lists a daily digest among its scheduled actions; Happy adds only asking, and being told, in the iMessage thread.

With the lookup on, each mail question also leaves the reader's transcript of that hand-off on the Mac (archived an hour after it finishes and kept until the disk budget evicts it, unless the optional 30-day setting of the wave A runbook is switched on) and the answer in the parent's own chat transcript.
set.safety: Each reader holds private mail and reads outsiders' text, so it has no way out: only Gmail read tools, and two outputs: the scheduled text, which the jobs script addresses from the family file, and, once the lookup is on, its answer to its owner's own agent. One reader, connector and token per parent; the two parents are held apart by tool permissions, an explicit deny and two tests until the house-rules plugin exists. The lookup is the weaker half: once it is on, the parent's own agent is allowed the same three read tools so that the reader it starts can use them, and only its instructions and a count of its tool calls keep it from reading mail itself.
unverified: gog is not installed on this Mac; its flags (`--gmail-scope readonly` and `--services` on `gog auth add`, `--allow-tool` on `gog mcp`) come from the upstream docs and must be confirmed with `gog mcp --list-tools` and `gog auth add --help` on the installed version.

T1: that publishing the self-made Google sign-in app to In production keeps a read-only Gmail token alive past seven days on a personal, unverified app. One search by hand on day 1 and again on day 8 or later, before the rest is built on the token; Google's scope page marks gmail.readonly as a Restricted scope.

Whether each adult's token can sit in a folder of its own under the happy user: upstream says tokens use the platform keyring by default with a file backend for headless hosts; splitting them with a per-adult GOG_HOME is an inference from the paths doc. The wave A runbook read upstream's source: a separate folder does not separate keyring entries, so it keeps each sign-in in happy's login Keychain under a namespace of its own and starts gog through a short wrapper; Tony's yes to both is asked at its step A4.

T2: that the minimal tool profile plus a per-agent allow shows each reader exactly one account server and shows it to no other agent (except that parent's own agent once its lookup is on, which is allowed the three tools on purpose); the roadmap lists this as not yet confirmed on this version. The 'read the other parent's mail' canary is run both ways.

T5, the connector turn: whether a plugin's blocking check is called for connector tools at all and, since 13 Oct, whether it is told which agent is calling, for a parent's own agent and for a helper it started. The docs say 'every tool call in the run' (plugins/hooks/tool-policy.md:222) but no sentence names MCP tools. It decides whether the account-connector rule can be written when the house-rules plugin is first created.

Whether a parent's own agent can see or quote the 07:00 text when the parent replies to it: checked at go-live. If it can, mail text reaches that agent even with the lookup switched off, and Tony signs that as the same departure from the roadmap as the lookup.

For the lookup, T4: that a hand-off from the parent's agent to its own mail reader returns the answer in the same chat while agents cannot see each other's sessions; and that a reader started this way keeps its three Gmail tools, which is read from the installed code and has not been run.

For the lookup, the seeded mail: a planted mail that tells the reader to make the parent's agent search for, save or pass on something must cause no tool call on the parent's agent in three runs (the planted mail also asks that agent to search the mailbox itself, which it is allowed to do and told not to), and the other parent's agent must be refused the reader. If either lookup test fails, the lookup stays off and the morning text is unaffected.

Whether this OpenAI account will be approved for Zero Data Retention; until then the 30-day abuse-monitoring log applies to mail text sent to the model. The per-person provider setting that sends store false was verified in M1 and not re-read here.

That a parent's own agent, allowed the Gmail read tools for the hand-off, keeps to its instruction and never calls them itself: a behaviour, checked by its tool-call record at go-live and at the exit test, and not enforced until the house-rules plugin's check exists, and then only if test T5 allows that check.
corrections: The 9 Oct needs list omits the sandbox-layer gate: with sandbox mode 'all', MCP tools stay hidden unless `tools.sandbox.tools` names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130). The minimal profile does not allow MCP tools implicitly either (same file, lines 36 and 41).

'Memory off' is not one switch in the installed docs: memory search has a per-agent override (`agents.entries.*.memory.search`, `enabled`, docs/reference/memory-config.md:31 and :102), dreaming is plugin-wide (docs/concepts/memory.md:275), and `excludeSessions.hookExternalContentSources` only matches hook sessions (docs/reference/memory-config.md:667).

'Send pinned to owner' only applies when the mail agent runs its own scheduled or hook turn: when spawned from `

-main` it always loses `message` and `session_status` (docs/tools/subagents/tool-policy.md:23), so its allow list must not consist of `session_status` alone.
The 9 Oct needs list puts `openclaw models status --agent --probe` in the deploy checks; the installed doc says a direct probe needs the Gateway stopped (docs/cli/models.md:121).

The 9 Oct verifier note says gogcli has no read-only-only Gmail scope. The upstream command reference lists `--gmail-scope full|readonly|send|read-send` and says `--readonly` on `gog auth add` requests read-only OAuth scopes, so a read-only grant can be requested; the catalog's hedge 'if the installed version supports it' can be firmed up, pending a check on the installed binary.

The 9 Oct text treats the `

-gmail` wrapper as new code. Upstream gogcli ships a stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`) that exposes only read tools unless `--allow-write` is passed, so the config entry can run gog directly with an `--allow-tool` list and no wrapper.

The 9 Oct needs list stops at the per-agent allow list. With sandbox mode 'all' (Happy's setting) the installed docs add a second gate: MCP tools are filtered out unless `tools.sandbox.tools` also names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130).

13 Oct, read in the installed code while the wave A runbook was written: an agent started through `sessions_spawn` keeps only the tools its asker is allowed. The spawn tool passes the asker's allow list and deny list to the child, also for a different target agent (dist/sessions-spawn-tool-B5tfhM3J.mjs:3244), and they are applied as the last filter, 'inherited tools' (dist/conversation-tool-policy-pipeline-D3eQnHfK.mjs:74); the docs say 'inherited tool policy' still applies (docs/tools/subagents/nesting.md:13). The lookup as first written, with the Gmail tools denied on the parent's own agent, could not have worked.

13 Oct: the card said no wrapper is needed for gog. The wave A runbook starts gog through a ten-line wrapper, which gives each sign-in its own keyring namespace and points gog at the local proxy; and it found that 2026.9.7 rejects a hand-off time limit set under one agent, so the limit is the gateway-wide default.

13 Oct: the wave A runbook builds each 07:00 text as two jobs, Tuesday to Friday looking back one day and Monday looking back three, because a scheduled message cannot carry the weekday; this page counts them as one text.

13 Oct, from the installed docs: `subagents.allowAgents` only governs a hand-off that names its target; one that names none starts a copy of the asking agent ('Default: only the requester agent', docs/tools/subagents/thread-bound-sessions.md:74), and `subagents.requireAgentId` is what refuses it. The lookup sets both.

edits.note: Tony, 13 Oct: helpers follow one pattern, "Happy main agent hold tools, then dispatch sub-agent to narrow tool selection to do their specific work". Each parent's agent is therefore allowed `web_fetch` so that the helper it starts can fetch, and is told never to fetch a page itself; the safety note says what that changes.

set.how: First T4: one hand-off from Tony's agent to the helper, with a time limit, must return its answer in the same chat while agents still cannot see each other's sessions. Agent: a shared `research` agent from the family file: a fresh sandbox per conversation, memory search off, no accounts, `web_search` and `web_fetch` only, its own capped key. Each parent's agent adds `research` to its `subagents.allowAgents`, beside its own mail reader; `sessions_spawn` and `subagents.requireAgentId: true` are already set by the mail lookup, or are set here if the lookup is off; the time limit is the gateway-wide `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds`, because 2026.9.7 rejects that key under one agent. Under the pattern Tony said on 13 Oct he expects to adopt for every helper, each parent's agent is also allowed `web_fetch`, which it is denied today (in its tool list and its sandbox tool list): on 2026.9.7 an agent started by another keeps only the tools its asker is allowed (the asker's allowed tools and its denies are passed to the helper and applied last), so the helper could not fetch otherwise. The helper's own list, `web_search` and `web_fetch`, is what narrows the hand-off. Guardrails: both `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` keys unset, `tools.web.fetch.headers` empty, no fetch-provider plugin, `tools.web.fetch.useTrustedEnvProxy` off, `browser.enabled: false`, `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. One rule in the helper's AGENTS.md: give the link and the time fetched, show the page's own date when it has one, give a price or date only from a fetched page, say 'could not verify'. In each parent's AGENTS.md the 'cannot open links' line becomes the hand-off rule: never fetch a page yourself, hand it to the helper, and what a task may carry; its smoke-eval case changes too. Four planted eval cases; in each, a fetch by the parent's own agent counts as a failure. Tony's agent first, Jordan's a day later. No plugin and no house-rules rule in this wave; when the house-rules plugin is created in wave C (planned there by Tony's choice of 13 Oct to keep the wave order), its who-may-call rule also covers `web_fetch` on a parent's own agent, if test T5 shows that the check is told which agent is calling; otherwise an instruction and the tool-call record stay the only guard.
caveats: The plain fetch runs no JavaScript and cannot log in, so such pages stay unread until the extra readers (F020) exist, and Happy says 'could not verify'. A slow lookup gets no 'on it' and no plain-words 'cancel that': the helper's built-in finish report is the only progress message, and a lookup ends at its time limit or at Tony's built-in stop.

If the hand-off test (T4) fails, the only documented alternative is session visibility `tree` for the whole gateway, which changes a signed-off setting and needs Tony's yes plus a re-run of the separation check.

The home-network block rests on the fetch tool resolving and pinning the address itself, so `tools.web.fetch.useTrustedEnvProxy` stays off and both private-network keys stay truly unset: an explicitly written `false` on the browser key turns hostname navigation into an allowlist and would stop the later research browser (F020).

Once the helper can fetch pages, neither the firewall nor the proxy can hold the gateway program to a list of hosts; they refuse home-network addresses and nothing more, so tool permissions, not the firewall, keep the mail readers and the shared agents off the web; a parent's own agent is allowed the fetch tool so that the helper can use it, and there an instruction and the planted tests do that work.

The answer rule and the rule on what goes into a task (the town and the children's ages yes, names and the school no) are prompt rules; nothing mechanical enforces them, and the planted eval cases are the only check. The roadmap's prompt-injection tripwire is not built with this card: by Tony's answer of 12 Oct it waits for local models.

The fetch tool's home-network check covers `web_fetch` only, so host-side helpers that take a web address (the summarize wrapper, watcher scripts) need their own scheme, host and resolved-address checks.
set.safety: The helper reads untrusted pages but holds no memory, accounts or family data, and cannot reach the home network. The roadmap's one remaining leak path stays open: a parent's agent holds private chats and writes the task text for a helper that can fetch any public address. A prompt rule and planted tests guard it; the helper's answer is treated as untrusted. Under that pattern the path is one step shorter: the parent's own agent is itself allowed the fetch tool, because a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed, and only its instructions and the planted tests keep it from fetching a page itself until the house-rules plugin's check exists in wave C, and after that only if test T5 allowed it.
unverified: That a cross-agent hand-off returns its result with agent-to-agent messaging off and session visibility set to self: the roadmap lists this as untested on 2026.9.7, and nothing was run here (T4).
The rule on what may go into the task text is a prompt rule; nothing mechanical enforces what a parent's agent writes into it.
Nothing in the installed stack enforces citations; it is a prompt rule the model can ignore, and the eval cases are the only check.
Whether page fetches pass through the outbound proxy once it is configured: the installed docs point both ways and nothing has been tried; it is read from the proxy's log when the gate is built.
The explicit-false behaviour of the browser policy was read in the installed source only; the docs do not describe it and it was not exercised.
How long a real lookup takes: nothing on the current stack runs longer than about 20 seconds, so whether an 'on it' line is ever needed is unknown until the hand-off exists.

That a helper started by a parent's agent that is allowed `web_fetch` keeps `web_search` and `web_fetch` and nothing else: read from the installed code, and first tried with the mail lookup in wave A (T4).

That a parent's own agent, allowed `web_fetch` for the hand-off, never fetches a page itself: an instruction, checked by the planted cases and its tool-call record, not a limit until wave C, and then only if T5 allows the coded rule.
corrections: The 9 Oct verifier notes advised turning the sandbox off for research; the installed docs say a sandboxed requester cannot spawn an unsandboxed target, so the catalog's final wording (keep mode all) is the only workable one.
A verifier note asked for research rules in AGENTS.md and SOUL.md; the installed docs say sub-agents keep only AGENTS.md, so every citation and no-login rule must be in that one file.

13 Oct: the card had each parent's agent denied `web_fetch` while its helper fetched. The installed code passes the asker's allowed tools and denies to the helper (dist/sessions-spawn-tool-B5tfhM3J.mjs:3244), so the asker must be allowed the tool as well.

edits.note: Tony, 13 Oct, the helper pattern: a tool the research helper uses must also be allowed on the parent's agent that starts it, so 'the helper only' becomes 'the helper, and each parent's agent for the hand-off's sake', with the coded rule keeping the parent's agent from using it.

set.how: Used by the research helper (F019) only; allowed on each parent's agent as well, for the hand-off. (1) Browser: the `browser` tool in the roadmap's sandbox browser container, on its own network with the home network blocked; `sandbox.browser.enabled` for the helper only, `allowHostControl` left false, `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`, the tool named in the helper's tool allow and sandbox tool allow lists. Under the 13 Oct pattern a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed, so the browser tool has to be allowed on each parent's agent as well for the hand-off to carry it; whether that also needs the sandbox browser switched on for the parent's agent is not known and is settled in this wave's plan. The image is built from a source checkout; if it cannot be built, the browser half is not built, and no host browser is used. (2) House-rules plugin, one rule: for the helper, a short allowlist of read-only browser action names (status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot); everything else, `act` and `upload` included, is blocked, failing closed. (3) Video and podcast text: a small connector on the Mac mini, allowed to the helper and, so that a hand-off can carry it, to each parent's agent (which is told never to call it itself), and denied by name elsewhere, wraps `summarize --extract --json` with `--firecrawl off`, no keys and no transcription fallback, and refuses home-network addresses itself. Planted-page cases join the eval suite.

The roadmap's browser network rule: the browser container on its own network with the home network blocked, and the test 'the browser cannot reach the home network' passing before go-live

The house-rules plugin (created here if no earlier feature needed it, and then with the account-connector rule of G015 as well): T5 is run for the `browser` tool, then the read-only action rule is live before the browser is switched on
The sandbox browser image built from a source checkout of the installed version

The `summarize` command-line tool installed from the admin account, with a firewall rule of its own; its connector is allowed to the helper and to each parent's agent that hands work to it, and the house-rules plugin's connector check (the rule the mail card, G015, adds) lets only the helper call it, if wave C's T5 allowed that rule
Tony provides at execution: two or three public pages the plain reader returned empty, and a video or podcast link he would want the main points of, as the first test cases

set.safety: The helper holds no private data, memory or accounts, and its browser never holds a login. Each parent's agent is allowed the same tools only so that the hand-off can carry them; the coded rule keeps that agent from using them itself (for the video reader only if wave C's T5 allowed the connector rule; otherwise an instruction and its tool-call record do). Only read-only browser actions pass, in code that fails closed; page scripts are off and the home network is out of reach, so bookings and CAPTCHA boxes stay out of reach. A task handed to it may carry the town and ages, never names or the school.

Whether the blocking check sees the browser call's action name, and whether it is given the helper's own id when the helper runs as a hand-off (T5; the names were read from the tool's schema, not seen in a live call).
Whether script-rendered pages can be read with no waiting, clicking or scrolling.

Whether the sandbox browser gives the helper a working `browser` tool with the top-level `browser.enabled` left false; the sandbox page says it is not required, the browser setup page says the tool needs it.
With open and navigate allowed, whether a link straight to a file is saved into the browser's downloads folder without the download action being called.

What `summarize` returns for a video without captions when no transcription is configured, and which of its flags exist in the installed version (`--youtube auto` appears in the bundled skill; check `summarize --help` after install).
Whether `summarize` can be made to send its calls through the outbound proxy; if not, its firewall rule and the wrapper's own address check are its only limits.

edits.note: Tony, 13 Oct, the helper pattern: each parent's agent is allowed the home agent's tools so that the hand-off can carry them, with a house-rules rule that lets only the home agent call them.

set.how: Step 1, read-only: a no-model job from the jobs script runs the `openhue` and `sonos` status commands on the Mac mini at the evening time Tony names and texts him only if something is on (`NO_REPLY` otherwise). Step 2, switching: a sandboxed `home` agent with no memory, no web tool and no message tool, on its own capped model key, reached by hand-off from each parent's agent, holds in-house tools that wrap the two command-line programs. Under the 13 Oct pattern each parent's agent is allowed the same tools, so that the hand-off can carry them, and is told to hand every command to the home agent. Hue: rooms and scenes by name, the bridge key kept in `~/.openhue/config.yaml`. Sonos: favourites, pause and volume, with one hard volume cap in the tool's code (Tony's number); no play-by-search. No quiet hours and no night cap; a room Tony wants left out is left out in the tool's code. The gateway's node process needs the macOS Local Network permission, or `--ip` per speaker. House-rules plugin: one rule, that only the home agent may call these tools (T5 decides whether it can be written); the cap sits inside the Sonos tool. Not built: Home Assistant, the TV, announcements.
set.safety: The home agent can change lights and speakers, so it holds no memory, family data, web tool or message tool, and is reached only by a bounded hand-off. Each parent's agent, which reads outside content, is allowed the same tools for the hand-off's sake; the house-rules rule, or an instruction alone if that rule cannot be written, keeps it from switching anything itself. Its tools' code offers only named rooms and scenes, favourites, pause and volume under a hard cap, and has no command for locks, garage, alarm or gate. The evening check runs no model and switches nothing.
unverified: Philips Hue's own local API documentation sits behind a developer login and was not opened; only the OpenHue CLI pages were.
Whether the gateway needs the Local Network permission for plain HTTPS to the bridge; the bundled skills document it only for Sonos discovery.
That the two programs report 'on' states in a form a short script can parse reliably; neither is installed.
That a hand-off to the home agent returns its result to the parent's agent (T4, first tried with the research helper, F019).
That a no-model job run by Happy's scheduler can reach the bridge and the speakers on the home network once the firewall blocks programs by default.
That the house-rules check is told which agent calls an in-house tool, so that a parent's own agent can be blocked from the tools it only holds for the home agent (T5).
caveats: This switches things in the house, so the volume cap is in the tool's code and not in the prompt. The number is Tony's starting value, not a sourced one.
Neither command-line tool is installed, and the bridge and the two speakers come from the 9 Oct scan and were not re-checked.
Favourites only: play-by-search is left out, because auto-playing the first search hit has no content filter.

Every command is two model turns, because the parent's agent hands it to the home agent. Each parent's agent is allowed the tools only so that the hand-off can carry them (Tony, 13 Oct); letting it call them itself would be one turn and is not done.
No quiet hours and no night cap: a parent's own late command is carried out. The Hue app can already switch lights at a set time, so the evening text is a nudge, not the switching.
Home Assistant, TV control and spoken announcements are not built.

edits.note: What the wave A runbook's jobs script does, where it differs from the card: a job declared again under the same key is updated in place if T3 confirms it, and a test job is declared with --no-deliver.

set.how: Config first: `cron.failureAlert` with Tony's handle as its destination, `cron.skipMissedJobs: true`, `cron.triggers.enabled: false`. Then test T3: happy-inspect gains one read-only line, `automations list --all --json`, and one throwaway job is added twice under the same `--declaration-key` with a changed message; one job afterwards means one add line per job, two means a name-keyed comparison is kept. Then one short checked-in jobs script, applied through the deploy path as the happy user. Every real job the script declares (not T3's throwaway probes) carries `--agent`, `--tz` and `--timeout-seconds`; a job whose text is delivered also carries `--to` (the owner's handle read from family.json5, never typed in) and `--announce`, and a test job that must send nothing is declared with `--no-deliver`. A job that calls the model also carries an explicit `--tools` list and no `--light-context`, so the hard rules load on every run; its message holds its rules: begin with the job's label, answer `NO_REPLY` when there is nothing to say. A text that needs no model is a `--command-argv` job. Something for both parents is two jobs, one each. No house-rules rule.
caveats: Failed-job alerts reach Tony as an iMessage from Happy, a deliberate exception to his 'alerts by ntfy' decision: OpenClaw's chat notice carries only a tidied cause, while its webhook would post the raw error text to an outside push service. If iMessage itself is down, the existing Grafana alerts still reach him by ntfy.

Alerts start after 2 failures in a row with a 1-hour cooldown. A recurring job is switched off after 10 failures in a row and then disappears from the default job list, which is why the inspect line lists every job, disabled ones included. Without a time limit of its own a model job is bounded only by a 60-minute watchdog, so the script sets one on every job.

Switching script triggers off does not stop the no-model jobs that other cards add through this script: OpenClaw's docs list a command job as a separate kind from the script payloads, condition triggers and stream schedules that the switch turns off.

After a reboot with FileVault locked nothing fires and nothing alerts; the healthchecks dead-man switch stays the only signal for a Mac that is off. One-off reminders still catch up after an outage even with missed runs skipped.

Given up with this form: per-person on and off switches in the family file, automatic clean-up of jobs that no longer match it, and any enforced daily cap or quiet hours. A changed job is applied again by the script if test T3 shows that a job declared again under the same key is updated in place (the wave A runbook read that in the installed code); otherwise it is edited by hand; to quieten Happy, Tony switches a job off or a parent silences the thread on the phone. The comparing generator comes back when the script holds more jobs than can be read at a glance.

Reminders Tony sets in chat (F007) are jobs outside the script; the inspect listing shows them beside the scripted ones. The script creates Jordan's jobs too, so her scheduled texts need no command right of her own.
